titleEn: The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood
author: James Gleick
introFa: کتاب «The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood» نوشته James Gleick یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON INFORMATION THEORY, VOL. 57, NO. 9, SEPTEMBER 2011 6333 1948, Shannon was well aware of (1) as the expression for the statistical mechanical entropy in the quantum setting. The description of the laws of physics has become increasingly prob- abilistic, and consequently more dependent on the role of information, or as Wheeler put it, with a hefty dose of poetic license: it from bit. Con- versely, the imperialistic instincts latent in the physics community cou- pled with Shannon’s “original sin” of borrowing a quantity from statis- tical mechanics made it inevitable that some would decree that infor- mation is physical. How our community has remained aloof from those slogans and debates, and, in fact, has developed a culture of steering clear of ventures beyond our original and natural habitat, would have made for a good side story. Thankfully, Gleick avoids promoting Norbert Wiener to the exag- gerated and distorted role that he occupies in all too many information theory histories, and, in particular, the balderdash that Wiener was to analog information what Shannon was to digital information. In Cy- bernetics (published contemporaneously with A Mathematical Theory of Communication), Wiener credits von Neumann with suggesting that (the negative of) the differential entropy of a density function f1 is “a reasonable measure of the amount of information associated with the curve f1(x),” maximizes (minimizes) it under a variance constraint, and considers the difference between unconditional and conditional differential entropies. In his autobiography I am a Mathematician, Wiener went on to write “the Shannon–Wiener deﬁnition of quantity of information (for it belongs to the two of us equally).” Unfortunately, both Shannon and Wiener referred to differential entropy as “entropy” so it is not surprising that Gleick fails to make the crucial point that differential entropy, unlike (2), is not a measure of information nor does it have an operational meaning (i.e., it is not the answer to an optimization problem of interest to the engineer). In fact, there is no evidence that Wiener ever grasped the notion, at the heart of information theory, of operational meaning lent by a coding theorem. Among all the heroes in The Information, one actually had been cer- tiﬁed as such (as Hero of Socialist Labor): Andrei Kolmogorov, who takes center stage in The Sense of Randomness, the excellent brief chapter devoted to algorithmic complexity. Gleick relates some of the major nuggets that tie the great Russian academician to information theory: his enthusiastic embrace (contrasting with his cold disdain for cybernetics) of Shannon’s paper, initially viewed as suspect by hard- core mathematicians on both sides of the Atlantic; his foundation of the ﬁrst mathematical school of information theory; his import of entropy into ergodic theory; and his deﬁnition of -entropy. A notable omission is Kolmogorov’s pioneering introduction of the notion of universal data compression. A subject whose founding paper states in its second paragraph: [The] semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem was bound to meet with less than a universal welcome. With admirable scholarship and keen sense of humor, Gleick captures the dismal recep- tion accorded to information theory by the social scientists: no seman- tics, meaningless beep beeps, the horror! The social science take on information/communication receives plenty of attention, with a liberal sprinkling of quotes by Marshall McLuhan, and whole chapters de- voted to the data deluge and to memes. Genes are to living organisms what memes are to thoughts, and therefore, subject to the evolutionary dictum of the survival of the ﬁttest—the Journal of Memetics was an early victim. There are many other fascinating side histories to be found in The Information, such as those of writing, the dictionary, Wikipedia and its paper forefathers, the DNA code, cryptography, and quantum in- formation/computing. But let us ﬁnally get on with the super-hero of the story. The Information makes a courageous effort to elevate Claude Shannon from his underrated status in the mainstream popular percep- tion of the history of science. Superbly researched, Gleick chronicles Shannon’s early years in Michigan; his graduate studies at MIT in- cluding the most important Master’s thesis of the century, his work on the differential analyzer, and his unpublished doctoral thesis on an algebra for genetics; his sojourn at the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton; his work on cryptography, and the gestation of A Math- ematical Theory of Communication at Bell Labs.2 Claude Shannon’s marriages to Norma Levor and Betty Moore, as well as his passion for gadgets, unicycling, and juggling, get their dues. Also mentioned are his contributions to the design of computers with unreliable compo- nents, to the max-ﬂow min-cut theorem, and to programming a ma- chine to play chess. But Shannon disappears from the story abruptly. The reader hopes, in vain, to ﬁnd out what ever happened to the genius who, in his early thirties, revolutionized the world. If anything, Gleick reinforces the lay misconception that Shannon’s salient contribution is his introduction, or rediscovery, of entropy. Nothing is said on the key role of measuring with bits not just likeli- hood but dependence. Moreover, Gleick fails to make the point that information theory is about theorems, rather than deﬁnitions; that it is about posing, and answering, questions on the best performance of algorithms for information compression and transmission and beyond. The reader is told about redundancy and the Shannon limits, but why is channel capacity indeed more relevant to Qualcomm than the speed of light is to Ferrari? In view of his obvious gifts, I wish Gleick had attempted a lay nar- rative of what we have learned since 1948 about the Shannon limits themselves (or, in the language of this Transactions, Shannon theory), and of those problems which remain stubbornly elusive. Along the way, he may have uncovered the cult of the pretty formula that we, the People of the Article, profess, and how those formulas have a way to inspire engineers. Most unfortunately, particularly in view of Gleick’s engaging account of the various 19th century information technologies and his repute as a leading popularizer of modern science and engi- neering, The Information makes no effort to explain how technology has evolved in the last 63 years in pursuit of the Shannon limits. No attempt is made to elucidate the algorithms that convert images and sounds into bits. Or the captivating race to convert bits into sounds at faster and faster speeds to send data through the telephone wire. Nothing on the fascinating story that starts with Hamming and culmi- nates with sparse-graph codes. Ending with Huffman, the lossless data compression narrative misses one of the crown jewels of information theory: the magical Lempel–Ziv algorithm, implemented everywhere and conqueror of the Shannon source coding limit. Nothing on the re- naissance of information theory brought about by the wireless revo- lution. And how about some elementary iTheory for the iPhone? The reader would have loved to ﬁnd out that Shannon is the answer to the question: Why do more bars result in faster downloads? Although we are told that Shannon’s theory [. . .] led to compact discs and fax machines, computers and cyberspace, Moore’s law and all the world’s Sil- icon Alleys the reader leaves with the impression that information theory is very much a thing of 1948. We are going to need a bigger book. 2Likely based on his interview of Betty Shannon, Gleick reveals that Claude Shannon was among the last researchers to move from the Bell Labs New York city building in the West Village to the gigantic new facility in Murray Hill, NJ. So, in fact, information theory did not come into existence in the state that gave us the lightbulb, the transistor, the Morse code, FM, and color TV, but in the city that gave us abstract expressionism and hip hop.
